extracted.intended_audience: reporters covering city hall and local politics; journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters covering municipal councils and local political beats: how to gather, write, and present city-hall and political news accurately, clearly, and with appropriate judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasis on vocal aldermen
rubrics_metrics.description: "Emphasizing the aldermen who always will comment on a pending proposal is psychologically difficult to resist... these quick talkers may not be safe guideposts to the attitude of the whole council."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the most talkative members as representative of the whole council; seek broader signals of council sentiment rather than leaning on habitual commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance advance stories for editors and readers; avoid sensationalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter writes advance stories "for two audiences" — readers and the three editors — but must resist intensifying the advance merely to whet editors' appetites (e.g., predicting battles that won't happen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-hype or invent dramatic language in advance copy to impress editors; avoid predicting explosions or 'opening gun' language unless justified by facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain meeting call/agenda from city clerk
rubrics_metrics.description: Council meetings often have mumbled, rapid announcements; getting a copy of the call from the city clerk lets the reporter follow rapid-fire items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official agenda to keep track of items that are announced too quickly to note in the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to identify officials and speakers quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn aldermen by face rather than location; when private citizens testify, ask the city clerk or arrange for presiding officer to ask each speaker to identify himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive about identification early in the beat; accept initial confusion as normal and correct it by consulting staff and presiding officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'in committee' / executive sessions as closed and unreportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a reporter may be permitted to attend 'in committee' or executive sessions, accept them as completely closed meetings which you are not at liberty to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish what was said in closed sessions. If the device is abused, consider public-interest ways to expose overuse (see related guidance on anonymous tips), but respect confidentiality norms and legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master parliamentary procedure (Roberts/Cushing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing whether Roberts' or Cushing's manual of procedure governs the council is essential so the reporter can understand amendments and procedural maneuvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the applicable parliamentary manuals; without this knowledge a reporter cannot write coherent stories about tactical amendments, sneaks, or procedural tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand committee roles and tentativeness of recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees (standing and special) report to the council; their reports are tentative — the council may accept, reject, modify, or ignore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow committee actions closely; report committee decisions as tentative and track when items are referred back, delayed, or effectively killed by lack of a report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take abundant, organized notes (separate sheet per item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring plenty of scratch paper so you can use a separate sheet for each business item, then shuffle sheets to put the strong items at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid minimal note-taking that buries brief but important items in the middle of a sheet; organize notes by item to prevent overlooking short but powerful bits of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate lead: feature vs direct
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the news "calls for a 'feature in the first line'" or can stand on its own; analyze the story before selecting lead type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a feature lead to humanize dry, statistical, or technical reports; use a straight/direct lead when the news is strong and needs no fortification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone to seriousness; avoid facile or frivolous writing for substantial news
rubrics_metrics.description: Facile writing that jokes about serious municipal matters can be offensive because it trivializes important issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve light, humorous tones for appropriate subjects; treat substantial or serious municipal business with respectful, clear prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize complex facts up front (snapper lead) so readers get the gist
rubrics_metrics.description: For complicated 'money stories' or legal explanations, use a one-sentence 'snapper lead' that gives the essential point so a reader who reads only a few paragraphs obtains the gist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify and condense the central fact early; use a clear summary to make dense material accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present big news directly; avoid unnecessary fortification
rubrics_metrics.description: When news is big enough to stand on its own (example: resignation after 27 years), the standard, direct structure is the best presentation; unnecessary 'fortifying' provokes readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid decorative or delayed openings for inherently interesting news; be direct unless complexity requires clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long council meetings into several short stories and coordinate with make-up
rubrics_metrics.description: If a meeting generates far more copy than fits at the front, write a compressed lead/roundup plus separate detailed stories for major items; help the make-up editor by producing more short pieces and by providing a checklist of council stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer multiple half-column items over a few long pieces when the paper will have a 'council page'; supply the make-up editor with a list so stories are not misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous with background and tie back to earlier stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Protracted matters (e.g., hearings postponed repeatedly) require throwbacks to earlier stories so readers understand the history and do not misinterpret delays as 'red tape.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concise history and context in later developments so casual readers are not left confused and misled about municipal efficiency or integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain jargon, nomenclature, and technical situations in ordinary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often don't know terms like 'provisional list', 'Chapter 88', or 'overlay'; reporters must translate city-hall language into common talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When technical or statutory terms appear, follow them with plain-language explanations (even if longer) so at-a-glance readers understand the meaning immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, A-B-C rephrasing for complicated statutory language
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a full plain-language explanation may take more space, it is worth it because it makes complex material easier to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity over brevity when legal/financial mechanisms would confuse most readers; rephrase and define key terms and mechanisms step by step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid veiled ridicule; criticize directly and seriously when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridiculing government through over-connotative phrasing (e.g., 'the Great and General Court, in its infinite wisdom') may invigorate copy but damages democratic respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wish to criticize, do so plainly and substantively rather than by ridicule that undercuts readers' confidence in government institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use style-sheet choices to reflect respect for government institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigning for capitalization (e.g., 'Supreme Court' vs 'supreme court') can affect readers' perception of governmental seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider advocating for style-sheet changes that present government bodies with appropriate formality and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let brief sensational quarrels dominate the story; keep the substantive outcome foremost
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'ten-second' personal quarrel should not be lifted into the lead at the expense of answering the readers' primary question (e.g., 'Do we get the softener or don't we?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include colorful exchanges as color, but lead with the council's action or decision and place quarrels in proper perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interpretation sparingly in political reporting; avoid premature forecasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Political writing often explains and interprets, but reporters should not interpret or forecast before they have learned enough; the more experienced the reporter, the more objective the writing should remain until complexity demands interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'guessing tomorrow's weather' about political outcomes; reserve interpretation for when context and background justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulate among politicians and cultivate background knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: To pick up history and stage setting, the reporter must circulate among politicians of all parties, learn the habits, speech, history, reputation, and where they congregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build relationships and local knowledge so sources will talk and so you can judge the true significance of statements and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn which politicians are influential and which sources are reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should know which politicians actually wield influence (not just officeholders) and which politicians will give accurate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify power brokers, back-stagers, and dependable informants; don't assume formal position equals influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify the significance and context of speeches and tips from aides
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept at face value a printed speech or an aide's framing of an event; understand the background before expanding it into major copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check context and historical significance before turning a supplied speech into a big interpretive piece; consult background sources to assess importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand voting methods and how outcomes are recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: "Passed by voice vote" may be adequate for secondary actions; larger proposals may use hand-raising, standing counts, or recorded tallies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to the voting method used so you can accurately report the result and whether it was a definitive count or a voice/nominal vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anonymous sourcing cautiously to expose abuses of closed meetings when public interest demands
rubrics_metrics.description: If a council overuses 'in committee' secrecy, the reporter may 'drop hints' to a friendly alderman, receive anonymous accounts of what was said, print the exposure, and defend the decision ethically as aimed at restoring public business to public view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the public interest in disclosure against confidences and ethics; use anonymous tips to challenge excessive secrecy but be prepared to justify the step professionally.
